look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST · American black nightshade is an UNARMED, green herb with simple alternate ovate leaves and VERY SMALL white five-lobed star flowers, often in compact clusters. On mature plants, inspect the SMALL (~5–10 mm) SHINY PURPLE-BLACK BERRIES and the tiny green CALYX LOBES bent sharply BACK from the base of each ripe berry. Check SHORT, plump yellow anthers (~0.7–1.5 mm) with a hand lens or macro photo. Crucially: multiple black nightshade species look like this from a distance—green fruit or white petals alone cannot prove S. americanum.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Solanaceae / Solanum: alternate simple leaves, fused five-lobed star/rotate corollas, 5 poricidal anthers and berry fruits. Do not assume every Solanum is prickly; American black nightshade is unarmed.
best_field_traits: unarmed green annual to short-lived perennial, erect to spreading up to about 1.5 m
ALTERNATE simple ovate/elliptic leaves, typically 2–10.5 × 1–4.5 cm, smooth to slightly wavy or shallowly toothed
usually 3–10 tiny white flowers borne together on simple, often umbrella-like stalk groups
white five-lobed corolla, typically only 4–8 mm across (occasional larger variation)
five SHORT yellow anthers, about 0.7–1.5 mm long
green pea-size developing berries turning GLOSSY purple-black, approximately 5–10 mm wide
mature fruit calyx lobes tiny and STRONGLY REFLEXED (pointing backwards away from berry)
mature berry pedicels often ERECT or SPREADING, with the berry separating and leaving its stalk attached to plant
morphology_keys.habit: Green unarmed herb, annual to short-lived perennial, from small weed to loose branching plant about 0.3–1.5 m. Can be hairless to sparsely hairy; purple tint on stems is variable, not diagnostic.
morphology_keys.leaf: Simple ALTERNATE petiolate leaves, generally ovate/elliptic with pointed tip and base narrowing toward petiole; entire, shallowly wavy or sinuate-toothed edges; FNA typically 2–10.5 cm long and 1–4.5 cm wide. Leaf margins vary, so leaf alone cannot resolve the Morelloid group.
morphology_keys.flower: The tiny white five-pointed star-shaped COROLLA is about 4–8 mm wide (Flora of North America). Anthers are five, bright yellow, short and fairly plump, only approximately 0.7–1.5 mm long, dehiscing through small apical pores that elongate to slits. Flowers in small unbranched 3–10-flowered clusters, often arranged like a little umbrella from one short inflorescence axis. White flower alone not sufficient because other black-nightshade relatives are also white-flowered.
morphology_keys.fruit: Initially green berries mature to shiny purple-black, about 5–10 mm wide, held on erect to spreading fruit stalks (pedicels). Under mature fruit the small green CALYX LOBES are strongly REFLEXED—point backwards/away from the berry instead of hugging it. Fruiting berries often detach while pedicels remain; internal seed/stone-cell counts may be needed for truly close look-alikes.

field_terms.Reflexed: Bent backwards. In fruit, check the 5 little green sepals directly beneath the berry; on S. americanum they bend AWAY from the black fruit.
field_terms.Calyx: Collective sepals below flower or berry; calyx lobes here stay small, not the spiny enclosure of buffalobur.
field_terms.Anther: Yellow pollen-bearing part of stamen; American black nightshade has especially short, plump anthers. Measure with macro image/scale.
field_terms.Pedicel: Individual flower or berry stalk. Compare whether ripe fruit points outward/upward versus downward, and whether stalk remains after berry falls.
field_terms.Sclerotic granule / stone cell: Hard little body inside ripe berry, NOT a seed. Taxonomists use counts (often 2–4 in S. americanum versus more in several relatives). Only examine under appropriate lab precautions; don't taste fruit.
field_terms.Umbel-like: Several little fruit/flower stalks arise close together; an approximate field clue, not an assertion of a true umbel.

morphology_keys.habitat: Common in disturbed ground, gardens, shady margins, trails, damp or enriched soil. S. americanum is reported in Texas; exact Hays County nativity scoring remains a separate paused lane.
morphology_keys.management: Do not eat leaves or berries; potentially toxic glycoalkaloids and difficult Morelloid identifications make this inappropriate as a food-identification lesson. This is a field-ID plant, not a harvest recommendation. For restoration work, document plants before removal; avoid spraying desirable vegetation while making uncertain nightshade determinations.
crew_field_sequence: 1 · HABIT: Find unarmed green herb with simple ALTERNATE ovate leaves. If heavily prickly, go to buffalobur / western horsenettle / silverleaf lesson.
2 · FLOWER: Look for SMALL (<~1 cm) white five-lobed stars and very SHORT YELLOW anthers. Take a close macro with a ruler if available.
3 · GREEN FRUIT: Confirm tight groups of smooth round green berries from one inflorescence—these are IMMATURE and not yet a definitive species character.
4 · RIPE FRUIT: Seek BLACK glossy berries (~5–10 mm). Check the TINY CALYX LOBES bend sharply backward and away from fruit; take a macro from the side.
5 · FRUIT PEDICEL: Look at whether fruit stalks remain erect/spreading and stay when ripe berries drop. Compare with S. emulans where pedicels more often drop with fruit.
6 · CONFIRM: If fruit is matte, calyx hugs berry, or anthers are noticeably longer (>2 mm), compare S. emulans / S. nigrescens / S. nigrum rather than guessing S. americanum from 'black berries'.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: The hardest look-alikes are OTHER unarmed black-berried Solanum species, particularly S. emulans and S. nigrescens, not the large prickly yellow-fruited species. Distinguish with anther length, fruit gloss, reflexed versus appressed fruit calyx, and pedicel behavior.

field_matrix.flower: Small white stars, ~4–8 mm; SHORT anthers 0.7–1.5 mm
field_matrix.pedicels: Usually erect/spreading; fruit detaches and stalk generally remains
field_matrix.quick_rule: SHINY BLACK + backwards calyx + TINY anthers together.

field_matrix.flower: Small white; also SHORT thick anthers, overlap with S. americanum
field_matrix.berries: Dull to moderately shiny dark berry; often >5 hard stone cells
field_matrix.calyx: Calyx lobes APPRESSED to SPREADING, not markedly turned backward
field_matrix.pedicels: Often hang/drop with fruit on more reflexed pedicels
field_matrix.quick_rule: A difficult look-alike: matte fruit and calyx hugging base argue against S. americanum; fruit/stone cells help.

field_matrix.flower: Larger stars, typically ~10–15 mm; LONGER anthers ~2–3 mm
field_matrix.calyx: APPRESSED or spreading, not strongly reflexed
field_matrix.pedicels: Fruiting pedicels spreading/deflexed; may drop with berry
field_matrix.quick_rule: Longer anthers and dull fruit with calyx not curling sharply back.

field_matrix.flower: White flowers, generally larger reproductive parts; variable

not_reliable_alone: Black berries on a green herb: S. americanum, S. emulans, S. nigrescens, introduced S. nigrum and other Morelloids overlap.
White five-lobed flower: shared across black-nightshade relatives.
Green immature berries: not distinctive; wait for black ripe fruit where possible.
Single leaf shape or hairiness: highly variable.
Tiny reflexed calyx seen on one unripe berry: look for strongly reflexed lobes on mature berries and confirm flower anthers.
The older regional name S. ptychanthum (occasionally misspelled ptycanthum) is treated by FNA and modern Morelloid revision as a synonym of S. americanum, not an automatic second species card.

visual_comparison.title: American black nightshade: TINY white flower → SHINY black berries → BACKWARD calyx
visual_comparison.subtitle: Five exact-species real-photo views and two differently labeled look-alikes. The closest unarmed black-berried species are distinguished by anther measurements, calyx lobes, pedicels and fruit appearance.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: SMALL white stars, SHORT yellow anthers, SHINY BLACK berries, SMALL calyx lobes REFLEXED away from fruit. Never identify from black berries alone.
visual_comparison.overlay_note: All photo arrows are separately generated by the learner, not embedded in photographs. External Commons photos are original links with creators and licenses credited; some were photographed outside Texas. The CC BY-SA image is displayed unchanged with a separate annotation layer and SA attribution retained. The exact-species source identification follows original photo labels and is not new voucher verification.

items.label: 1 — WHOLE PLANT: leaves and berry groups
items.image_role: Green unarmed branching herb with entire to shallow-toothed alternate leaves and small green fruit groups
items.caption: Original photo by Eurico Zimbres: follow the non-prickly stems through the green oval leaves and groups of small berries. All pictured berries are GREEN / immature, so this view shows habit but is not a mature-fruit confirmation.
items.why_it_matters: Separate unarmed, small-leaved black nightshade growth from big prickly Solanum; use mature berry calyx and flower-anther macros later.
items.creator: Eurico Zimbres

items.label: 2 — SMALL WHITE FLOWERS + green berries
items.image_role: Small white five-lobed flower near small clustered green fruits
items.caption: Already installed CC BY photo by Raúl A. Ruiz M. The upper white flower has tiny yellow anthers. The clusters below it are green IMMATURE berries. Be careful: this photograph does not show black ripe fruit or ripe reflexed calyx lobes.
items.why_it_matters: See actual scale and grouping, but do not overidentify the close Morelloid species until mature fruit and anther details are examined.
items.creator: Raúl A. Ruiz M.

items.label: 3 — FLOWER MACRO: white corolla and SHORT anthers
items.image_role: High-resolution small white flower with short plump yellow anthers, on flower stalks
items.caption: Macro photograph from Australia, credited to Harry Rose. The white star (joined corolla lobes) surrounds the little plump, clustered yellow ANTHERS. In American black nightshade these anthers are short—usually about 0.7–1.5 mm. The long green stalk is a flower-bearing axis/pedicel, not a floral style. Small white flowers alone do NOT distinguish every member of the black-nightshade group. Arrow target verification: white corolla lobe of central flower, yellow anther cluster at its center, and the narrow pedicel supporting the hanging unopened flower bud at lower right.
items.why_it_matters: Short anthers are among the most reliable measured splits from S. nigrescens; exact 1 mm measurement still needs scale/hand lens.
items.creator: Harry Rose
items.photo_status: 2026-10-20: Retargeted three nondestructive anatomy overlays from user's iPhone screenshot of exact Commons photo: isolated upper-left white corolla lobe (43,33), yellow anther cluster of central flower (48,50), and narrow stalk of drooping bud (67,59). Label updated to 'Bud pedicel (stalk)'. Source photo and creator/license unchanged; final published phone check pending.

items.label: 4 — RIPE FRUIT: glossy BLACK berries and backward calyx
items.image_role: Full ripe black berry cluster, glossy berry surface, small reflexed sepals at berry bases
items.caption: The berries are actually BLACK and highly glossy, not just dark green. At the base of the upper berry the small green sepals bend backwards away from the fruit; these are calyx LOBES, not little leaves on the stem. The thin fruit stalks (pedicels) remain relatively erect to spreading. Credit Filo gèn', CC BY-SA 4.0; original photo unmodified, learner arrows overlaid separately. Photographed outside the Hays region.
items.why_it_matters: Check GLOSS and BACKWARD calyx together against other black nightshades, not merely a black fruit color.
items.creator: Filo gèn'

items.label: 5 — CALYX MACRO: sepals reflex away from berry
items.image_role: Single ripe dark berry with clearly reflexed calyx lobes under fruit
items.caption: Best single view of a key distinction: the shiny mature berry sits ABOVE a small green calyx whose sepals curl downward/away from the fruit, rather than hugging it. Compare S. emulans or S. nigrescens, which typically have calyx lobes appressed or spreading, and less glossy mature fruit. Photo from Australia, attributed to Harry Rose.
items.why_it_matters: This is the cleanest photograph for teaching the small bent-back calyx lobes of a mature berry.
items.creator: Harry Rose

items.label: 6 — LOOK-ALIKE: Silverleaf has a large flower and silvery leaves
items.image_role: Different species with narrow densely gray-silver foliage
items.caption: THIS IS SILVERLEAF NIGHTSHADE, NOT AMERICAN BLACK NIGHTSHADE. Gray/silver leaves, large lavender flowers, and exposed yellow ripe berries, unlike green unarmed little white-flowered S. americanum.
items.why_it_matters: A useful quick split before inspecting closely similar black-berried unarmed Solanum species.
items.creator: Alex Abair

items.label: 7 — LOOK-ALIKE: Buffalobur has an enclosing SPINY calyx
items.image_role: Different species with spiny fruiting calyces
items.caption: THIS IS BUFFALOBUR, NOT AMERICAN BLACK NIGHTSHADE. Its brown/green globes are spiny enlarging calyces concealing fruits; S. americanum has exposed shiny BLACK berries with TINY non-prickly reflexed sepals.
items.why_it_matters: Shows that 'calyx' can be a little curled-back green collar or a huge spiny enclosure depending on the species.
items.creator: Dcrjsr
